shortExplanation: The denominator is $4\cdot500=2000$, so the quotient is $500$.
detailedSteps: The numerator is $1000^2=1000000$. Dividing by 2000 gives 500.
keyIdeas: Factor the difference of squares
commonMistakes: Subtracting the two bases before squaring instead of factoring their difference of squares.
difficultyNotes: Nearby squared numbers are easiest to compare by their sum and difference.

shortExplanation: Both parts contain $xy-1$, leaving $x/y$. The stated domain makes this cancellation valid.
detailedSteps: The numerator is $x-1/y=(xy-1)/y$, while the denominator is $y-1/x=(xy-1)/x$.

The source assumes $x
e0$, $y
e0$ and $y-1/x
e0$. The last condition means $xy-1
e0$, so the quotient simplifies to $((xy-1)/y)(x/(xy-1))=x/y$.
keyIdeas: Cancel only on the original nonzero domain
commonMistakes: Canceling the common factor without checking that it is nonzero in the original expression.
difficultyNotes: A cancellation must preserve the domain on which the original quotient is defined.

shortExplanation: The smallest allowed prime is eleven, so the smallest allowed composite is $11^2=121$.
detailedSteps: A composite integer greater than one has at least two prime factors when counted with multiplicity. With no prime factor below ten, each is at least eleven.
Therefore the integer is at least $11\cdot11=121$. This value itself qualifies, and it lies in $120<n\le130$, choice C.
keyIdeas: Use the least permitted prime factor
commonMistakes: Treating eleven itself as composite, or using ten even though ten has smaller prime factors.
difficultyNotes: The minimum composite is the square of the minimum permitted prime.

shortExplanation: The circle’s vertical symmetry line is $6.5$ units from the rectangle’s left side, making the lower chord seven units long.
detailedSteps: Use the rectangle’s left side as horizontal coordinate zero. The upper chord starts at $B$ with coordinate four and ends at $C$ with coordinate $4+5=9$. Its midpoint has coordinate $13/2$.
The perpendicular bisectors of the two parallel horizontal chords pass through the same circle center. Thus the lower chord has the same midpoint coordinate.
The actual lower left endpoint $E$ has coordinate three. Its right endpoint has coordinate $2(13/2)-3=10$, and $EF=10-3=7$.
keyIdeas: Align the midpoints of parallel circle chords
commonMistakes: Assuming the two parallel chords have equal lengths instead of equal midpoint coordinates.
difficultyNotes: The rectangle makes the chord directions parallel; no radius or rectangle height is needed.

shortExplanation: The positive threshold is $5^{3/2}$, between eleven and twelve, so the largest integer is eleven.
detailedSteps: For a positive candidate, $n^{200}<5^{300}$ is equivalent to $n^2<5^3=125$. Since $11^2=121<125<144=12^2$, the largest positive integer is eleven.
Negative integers may also satisfy the original even-power inequality, but none can exceed eleven. Thus eleven is the largest integer in the entire original domain.
keyIdeas: Compare the exact positive threshold
commonMistakes: Rounding the real threshold upward even though the inequality is strict.
difficultyNotes: An even power allows negative inputs without changing the greatest positive solution.

shortExplanation: The ratios are $b:g:t=27:9:1$, so the total is $37b/27$.
detailedSteps: The given relationships are $b=3g$ and $g=9t$, hence $b=27t$. Therefore $b+g+t=27t+9t+t=37t$.
Substituting $t=b/27$ gives the total $(37/27)b$, which is the listed expression in choice B.
keyIdeas: Express every group in one count unit
commonMistakes: Adding the ratio multipliers without first expressing all counts in the same unit.
difficultyNotes: Using the teacher count as one ratio unit keeps both multipliers visible.

shortExplanation: Dave covers $108000$ centimeters, and Jack covers $6000$ centimeters per minute, so Jack needs eighteen minutes.
detailedSteps: Dave’s speed is $90\cdot75=6750$ centimeters per minute. In sixteen minutes he travels $6750\cdot16=108000$ centimeters.
Jack’s speed is $100\cdot60=6000$ centimeters per minute. On the same route, his time is $108000/6000=18$ minutes.
keyIdeas: Use equal distance rather than equal step count
commonMistakes: Comparing steps per minute alone while ignoring the different step lengths.
difficultyNotes: Distance per minute is the product of step frequency and step length.

shortExplanation: The height is three; the two side projections are three and $\sqrt3$, giving $DC=8+\sqrt3$.
detailedSteps: The right side has length $3\sqrt2$ and meets the lower base at $45^\circ$. Its vertical and horizontal projections are both three, so the trapezoid’s height is three.
The left side meets the base at $60^\circ$. Its horizontal projection is $3/\tan60^\circ=\sqrt3$.
The pictured lower base extends beyond the upper base on both sides. Therefore $DC=3+AB+\sqrt3=3+5+\sqrt3=8+\sqrt3$.
keyIdeas: Add both horizontal projections to the upper base
commonMistakes: Subtracting a side projection even though both actual base angles make the lower base wider.
difficultyNotes: Dropping perpendiculars separates a trapezoid into a rectangle and two right triangles.

shortExplanation: The integer is $128\cdot10^{25}$, which has twenty-eight digits.
detailedSteps: This is the three-digit integer 128 followed by twenty-five zeros, so it has $3+25=28$ decimal digits.
keyIdeas: Pair factors of two and five into powers of ten
commonMistakes: Counting twenty-five zeros as the total digit count, or failing to double the exponent when replacing four by two.
difficultyNotes: Exact powers of ten avoid numerical logarithm errors at digit boundaries.

shortExplanation: The two length-$\sqrt{10}$ sides meet at $-2+i$; completing the parallelogram gives $2-i$.
detailedSteps: Write the three points as $P=(1,2)$, $Q=(-2,1)$ and $R=(-1,-2)$. Their squared distances are $PQ^2=QR^2=10$ and $PR^2=20$. Thus $Q$ is the square vertex adjacent to both $P$ and $R$.
The fourth vertex is $S=P+R-Q=(2,-1)$, corresponding to $2-i$.
The four consecutive sides have squared length ten, and the two diagonals have squared length twenty. The two side vectors at $Q$ have dot product zero, verifying the constructed square.
keyIdeas: Identify the right-angle vertex among the three points
commonMistakes: Using one of the three points as the shared adjacent vertex without checking which pair forms the diagonal.
difficultyNotes: Three square vertices contain two equal sides and one diagonal, fixing their roles.

shortExplanation: One square-and-reciprocal pair multiplies the exponent by $-2$, so after $n$ pairs it is $(-2)^n$.
detailedSteps: A square followed by a reciprocal sends a nonzero value $u$ to $u^{-2}$. Reversing those two operations gives the same result, so either alternating starting order has the same pair map.
If the current expression is $x^e$, one pair changes it to $x^{-2e}$. Starting with exponent one, $n$ pairs give exponent $(-2)^n$. Therefore $y=x^{(-2)^n}$.
All powers involved have integer exponents, and the nonzero initial entry keeps each reciprocal defined even if that initial entry is negative.
keyIdeas: Track how each pair of operations changes the exponent
commonMistakes: Replacing repeated squaring by the linear exponent $2n$, or applying only one reciprocal sign to every pair.
difficultyNotes: Repeated composition acts on the exponent multiplicatively.

shortExplanation: The initial value two plus $2(1+\cdots+99)$ gives $9902$.
detailedSteps: To move from $a_1$ to $a_{100}$, use the recurrence for $n=1,2,\ldots,99$. Thus $a_{100}=2+2\sum_{n=1}^{99}n$.
The arithmetic sum is $99\cdot100/2=4950$. Therefore $a_{100}=2+9900=9902$.
keyIdeas: Sum exactly the ninety-nine increments
commonMistakes: Including the increment for $n=100$, which would instead advance to $a_{101}$.
difficultyNotes: The final index determines which increments are included.

shortExplanation: The denominator times $\sqrt2+\sqrt3-\sqrt5$ is exactly $2\sqrt6$, the numerator.
detailedSteps: Group the denominator as $(\sqrt2+\sqrt3)+\sqrt5$. Multiply it by the conjugate $(\sqrt2+\sqrt3)-\sqrt5$.
The product is $(\sqrt2+\sqrt3)^2-5=2+3+2\sqrt6-5=2\sqrt6$.
The original denominator is positive, so the quotient $2\sqrt6/(\sqrt2+\sqrt3+\sqrt5)$ equals $\sqrt2+\sqrt3-\sqrt5$.
keyIdeas: Use the conjugate of the combined radical term
commonMistakes: Negating all three radicals rather than only the last term of the grouped conjugate.
difficultyNotes: Combining two radicals before taking a conjugate can reveal the given numerator.

shortExplanation: The logarithm of the equation gives $(\log_{10}x)^2=1$, whose two positive roots have product one.
detailedSteps: The original logarithm requires $x>0$. Put $u=\log_{10}x$, so $x=10^u$. Taking base-ten logarithms of $x^{\log_{10}x}=10$ gives $u^2=1$.
Thus $u=1$ or $u=-1$, yielding $x=10$ or $x=1/10$. Both satisfy the original equation, and their product is one. No other real value lies in the logarithm’s domain and satisfies $u^2=1$.
keyIdeas: Take logarithms on the positive original domain
commonMistakes: Discarding the negative logarithm value even though it corresponds to the positive root $1/10$.
difficultyNotes: A positive base may have a negative logarithm without leaving the real domain.

shortExplanation: The equation is equivalent to $\cos5x=0$, and $x=18^\circ$ is a listed solution.
detailedSteps: Move the left side to the right: $\cos2x\cos3x-\sin2x\sin3x=0$. The cosine addition identity makes this $\cos(5x)=0$.
For $x=18^\circ$, the angle $5x$ is $90^\circ$, so the cosine is zero. This supplies the requested listed value; a full period classification is unnecessary because the question asks for one value.
keyIdeas: Recognize the cosine of the sum of the two angles
commonMistakes: Using the cosine difference identity, which has a plus sign between the sine product and cosine product.
difficultyNotes: The listed angle values establish degrees for this multiple-choice comparison.

shortExplanation: The four distinct roots form two reflected pairs, each summing to four, so their sum is eight.
detailedSteps: The given symmetry implies $f(r)=f(4-r)$ for every real $r$. Therefore reflection $r\mapsto4-r$ maps the four-element root set to itself.

Every nonfixed orbit consists of two roots whose sum is four. The only possible fixed root is two. It cannot belong to a four-element root set, because the other three roots could not all be partitioned into two-element orbits.
Thus there are two pairs and their total is $4+4=8$. This uses no continuity or polynomial assumption about $f$.
keyIdeas: Pair roots by reflection about two
commonMistakes: Assuming the roots occur in pairs about zero rather than about the source symmetry center two.
difficultyNotes: A finite symmetric root set can be summed without knowing the function’s formula.

shortExplanation: The hypotenuse segments are nine and sixteen, giving altitude twelve and triangle area $150$.
detailedSteps: Let $AH=t>0$. The right-triangle leg theorem gives $AC^2=AH\cdot AB=t(t+16)$. Hence $t^2+16t-225=0=(t-9)(t+25)$, and the positive length is $t=9$.
The hypotenuse is $AB=9+16=25$. The altitude satisfies $CH^2=AH\cdot HB=9\cdot16=144$, so $CH=12$.
The area is $AB\cdot CH/2=25\cdot12/2=150$. The resulting side lengths are 15,20,25, consistent with the original right triangle.
keyIdeas: Use the leg-projection relation on the hypotenuse
commonMistakes: Treating the segment sixteen as the entire hypotenuse, or accepting the negative quadratic root as a length.
difficultyNotes: An altitude to the hypotenuse turns the given partial segment into a quadratic length relation.

shortExplanation: There are four equidistant points, with different horizontal coordinates, so $x$ is not uniquely determined.
detailedSteps: Equal distance from the coordinate axes means $|x|=|y|$, so either $y=x$ or $y=-x$. The distance to the third line is $|x+y-2|/\sqrt2$.
On $y=x$, the condition is $|2x-2|=\sqrt2|x|$. Squaring gives $x^2-4x+2=0$, with $x=2\pm\sqrt2$. Both points $(x,x)$ satisfy all three distance conditions.
On $y=-x$, the third-line distance is $\sqrt2$, so $x=\pm\sqrt2$. These give the two points $(\sqrt2,-\sqrt2)$ and $(-\sqrt2,\sqrt2)$.
The original statement imposes no quadrant restriction. These four points have distinct horizontal coordinates, so the answer is not uniquely determined.
keyIdeas: Include every angle bisector of the two axes
commonMistakes: Selecting only the point inside the first-quadrant triangle when the source asks about the entire plane.
difficultyNotes: Distances are nonnegative and require absolute values in every quadrant.

shortExplanation: There are $236$ favorable subsets among $462$, giving $118/231$.
detailedSteps: Under the usual uniform subset model for the simultaneous random draw, all $\binom{11}{6}=462$ selections are equally likely. There are six odd labels and five even labels.
The sum is odd precisely when the selected odd-label count is one, three or five. The favorable total is $\binom61\binom55+\binom63\binom53+\binom65\binom51=6+200+30=236$.
Thus the probability is $236/462=118/231$. The uniform subset reading is the standard random-draw interpretation, not an extra sentence quoted as explicit source wording.
keyIdeas: Count subsets with an odd number of odd labels
commonMistakes: Assuming odd and even sums are equally likely despite the unequal odd and even label populations.
difficultyNotes: The parity of a sum depends only on how many odd summands it contains.

shortExplanation: The valid roots are $2$ and $-4/3$, so there are two distinct solutions.
detailedSteps: If $x\ge-1/2$, then $|2x+1|=2x+1$ and the equation becomes $|x+1|=3$. Its candidates are $x=2$ and $x=-4$, but only $2$ lies in this branch.
If $x<-1/2$, then $|2x+1|=-2x-1$, giving $|3x+1|=3$. Its candidates are $x=2/3$ and $x=-4/3$, and only $-4/3$ lies in this branch.
Both surviving values satisfy the original nested expression. The branches cover every real input, so the count is exactly two.
keyIdeas: Validate both levels of absolute-value branches
commonMistakes: Counting all four linear candidates without checking the inner absolute-value domain for each.
difficultyNotes: Nested absolute values require domain checks at the inner split as well as the outer sign.

shortExplanation: The second equation forces $c=1$ and $a+b=23$, leaving the two triples $(21,2,1)$ and $(1,22,1)$.
detailedSteps: The second equation factors as $c(a+b)=23$. Since all three integers are positive and $a+b\ge2$, primality forces $c=1$ and $a+b=23$.
The first equation is then $b(a+1)=44$. With $a=23-b$, it becomes $b(24-b)=44$, or $(b-2)(b-22)=0$.
The two possibilities are $(a,b,c)=(21,2,1)$ and $(1,22,1)$. Both are positive and satisfy both original equations; the prime factorization and quadratic branches exclude every other triple.
keyIdeas: Exploit the prime-valued factored equation first
commonMistakes: Allowing $c=23$ even though it would require two positive integers to have sum one.
difficultyNotes: A prime-valued product is more restrictive than either unfactored quadratic expression.

shortExplanation: The vertex coordinates satisfy $Y=c-aX^2$, and every real $X$ occurs.
detailedSteps: For $y=ax^2+tx+c$ with $a>0$, the vertex is $X=-t/(2a)$ and $Y=c-t^2/(4a)$. Eliminating $t=-2aX$ gives $Y=c-aX^2$.
As $t$ ranges over every real number, $X=-t/(2a)$ also ranges over every real number. Thus the locus is the entire downward-opening parabola $Y=c-aX^2$, not just part of it.
keyIdeas: Eliminate the parameter and prove full coverage
commonMistakes: Stopping after obtaining a curve equation without checking whether all its points are attained by the parameter.
difficultyNotes: A parameter elimination describes the full locus only when the parameter range covers it.

shortExplanation: The sine sum and cosine sum share $2\cos5^\circ$, leaving $\tan15^\circ$.
detailedSteps: Use the sum identities: $\sin10^\circ+\sin20^\circ=2\sin15^\circ\cos5^\circ$ and $\cos10^\circ+\cos20^\circ=2\cos15^\circ\cos5^\circ$.
Both canceled factors are nonzero. The ratio is therefore $\sin15^\circ/\cos15^\circ=\tan15^\circ$.
keyIdeas: Cancel the common sum-to-product factor
commonMistakes: Distributing the quotient across the two sums to form a sum of tangents.
difficultyNotes: A ratio of angle sums often simplifies using their mean and half-difference.

shortExplanation: The two real-root conditions force $a\ge4$ and $b\ge2$; $(a,b)=(4,2)$ attains sum six.
detailedSteps: The discriminants must be nonnegative: $a^2-8b\ge0$ and $4b^2-4a\ge0$. Hence $a^2\ge8b$ and $b^2\ge a$.
Because $a,b>0$, squaring the first inequality gives $a^4\ge64b^2\ge64a$. Dividing by positive $a$ yields $a^3\ge64$, so $a\ge4$. The second inequality now gives $b\ge\sqrt a\ge2$.
Thus $a+b\ge6$. At $a=4,b=2$, both quadratics are $x^2+4x+4=(x+2)^2$, so both have real roots and the bound is attained. The minimum is six.
keyIdeas: Combine both discriminants into a global lower bound
commonMistakes: Using only one quadratic’s discriminant, or obtaining a bound without constructing parameters that attain it.
difficultyNotes: Combining constraints can yield separate sharp lower bounds for two parameters.

shortExplanation: The side sum is six and the pairwise-product sum is eleven, so the squared diagonal is fourteen.
detailedSteps: Let the positive side lengths be $a,b,c$. The total edge length gives $4(a+b+c)=24$, hence $a+b+c=6$. The surface area gives $2(ab+bc+ca)=22$, hence $ab+bc+ca=11$.
Every space diagonal has squared length $a^2+b^2+c^2=(a+b+c)^2-2(ab+bc+ca)=36-22=14$. Thus its length is $\sqrt{14}$ centimeters.

The conditions are consistent: side lengths one, two and three have the required edge total and surface area. Individual dimensions need not be uniquely determined for this diagonal length to be fixed.
keyIdeas: Use symmetric sums to recover the diagonal
commonMistakes: Declaring the diagonal undetermined merely because the three side lengths have not been individually solved.
difficultyNotes: A geometric quantity may be determined by invariants even when the underlying dimensions are not.

shortExplanation: The base $BD$ is half the horizontal coordinate of A, while E’s height supplies the inverse factor; the area is half of $24$.
detailedSteps: Use the actual pictured incidence $E\in AB$ and put $B=(0,0)$, $C=(c,0)$, $A=(a,h)$ with positive $c,h$. The midpoint is $M=(a/2,h/2)$, so its perpendicular foot is $D=(a/2,0)$.
The line $AB$ has equation $y=(h/a)x$. Since $EC$ is perpendicular to the horizontal base, $E=(c,ch/a)$.

The original triangle has area $ch/2=24$. Triangle $BED$ has base $BD=a/2$ and altitude $ch/a$, hence area $(a/2)(ch/a)/2=ch/4=12$. The pictured bounded locations and obtuse arrangement are consistent with $c<a<2c$.
keyIdeas: Track midpoint projection and the pictured line intersection
commonMistakes: Using M’s height as E’s height, or ignoring the source figure’s incidence of E on AB.
difficultyNotes: Coordinate projection keeps the different midpoint and intersection roles separate.

shortExplanation: Writing $AC=t$ leads to $t^4=2t$, so the positive length is $\sqrt[3]{2}$.
detailedSteps: Let $AC=t>0$ and $AB=u>0$. Since $D$ lies on $AC$ with $DC=1$, its distance from $A$ is $t-1$. The right triangle $ABD$ gives $u^2+(t-1)^2=BD^2=1$. Thus $u^2+t^2=2t$.
The original right triangle has altitude $AF$ to its hypotenuse. The leg-projection theorem gives $AC^2=BC\cdot FC$. Because $FC=1$, we have $BC=t^2$. Pythagoras then gives $u^2+t^2=BC^2=t^4$.
Combining yields $t^4=2t$. Positive $t$ excludes zero, leaving $t^3=2$ and $t=\sqrt[3]{2}$.

This value is between one and two, so $AD=t-1>0$, and $u^2=2t-t^2>0$. The hypotenuse is $t^2>1$, placing the altitude foot with $FC=1$ on the bounded side; all three specified unit lengths are realized.
keyIdeas: Combine a unit cevian with the right-triangle projection theorem
commonMistakes: Treating the given unit projection FC as the entire hypotenuse, or retaining the zero solution of the eliminated equation.
difficultyNotes: Two different right triangles express the same squared side sum in terms of AC.

shortExplanation: The common squarefree part is $31$, and the two positive square-root multipliers sum to eight, giving three pairs.
detailedSteps: Squaring once gives $1984=x+y+2\sqrt{xy}$. Thus $\sqrt{xy}$ is rational; the square root of an integer can be rational only if it is an integer. Consequently $xy$ is a perfect square.
Write $x=dr^2$ and $y=ds^2$ with the same squarefree positive integer $d$ and integers $0<r<s$. Then the original equation becomes $1984=d(r+s)^2$.
The prime factorization $1984=2^6\cdot31$ forces the squarefree part $d=31$ and $r+s=8$. The possibilities are $(r,s)=(1,7),(2,6),(3,5)$.
They give $(x,y)=(31,1519),(124,1116),(279,775)$. Each satisfies the original radical sum and the strict order, so there are three distinct pairs.
keyIdeas: Separate the common squarefree part of the radicals
commonMistakes: Assuming x and y must themselves be perfect squares rather than allowing a shared squarefree factor.
difficultyNotes: Prime-exponent parity describes when two square roots can combine into a single radical.

shortExplanation: The allowed slopes satisfy $m^2-6m+1\le0$, so the maximum is $3+2\sqrt2$.
detailedSteps: The locus is the circle with center $(3,3)$ and radius $\sqrt6$. Every point has $x\ge3-\sqrt6>0$, so the requested ratio $m=y/x$ is defined throughout the circle.
The line $y=mx$ meets that circle exactly when its distance from the center is at most the radius: $|3m-3|/\sqrt{m^2+1}\le\sqrt6$. Squaring simplifies to $m^2-6m+1\le0$.

Therefore $3-2\sqrt2\le m\le3+2\sqrt2$. The upper endpoint is attained because equality gives a tangent line to the actual circle. Its tangency point has $x=3(1+m)/(1+m^2)>0$ and $y=mx$, so the maximum is valid on the original domain.
keyIdeas: Find the maximum slope through the origin tangent to the circle
commonMistakes: Dividing without checking whether the circle crosses x=0, or maximizing y independently of x.
difficultyNotes: The ratio of coordinates is a line slope, so its extremum occurs at a supporting tangent.

shortExplanation: The weighted sum has magnitude $9/(2\sin20^\circ)$, so its reciprocal is $2\sin20^\circ/9$.
detailedSteps: The given $w=\cos40^\circ+i\sin40^\circ$ is a primitive ninth root of unity, with $w^9=1$ and $w\ne1$. Thus $w+w^2+\cdots+w^9=0$.
Let $S=w+2w^2+\cdots+9w^9$. Subtracting $wS$ from $S$ gives $(1-w)S=(w+w^2+\cdots+w^9)-9w^{10}=-9w$.
Since $|w|=1$, we have $|S|=9/|1-w|$. The unit-circle chord from one to w has length $2\sin20^\circ$, so $|S|^{-1}=|1-w|/9=(2/9)\sin20^\circ$. The nonzero chord also confirms $S\ne0$.
keyIdeas: Shift the weighted root-of-unity sum once
commonMistakes: Differentiating the constraint w^9=1 as though it held for all complex w, instead of subtracting the actual finite polynomial sums.
difficultyNotes: A single shift turns increasing coefficients into an ordinary geometric sum.
